citations.narrative:
The two outdoor enclosures housing two ring-tailed lemurs, one common lemur, and one rhesus macaque do not have a
sufficient perimeter fence. These enclosures are outside the facilities’ eight foot perimeter fence and do not have a
complete perimeter fence at least 6 feet tall fully around these enclosures.
An insufficient perimeter fence can allow unwanted animals or people to enter the facility and potentially harm the animals
within. The perimeter fence must be constructed so that it protects nonhuman primates by restricting unauthorized
humans, and animals the size of dogs, skunks, and raccoons from going through it or under it and having contact with the
nonhuman primates. It must be of sufficient height (at least six feet high) to keep unwanted species out. It must be of
sufficient distance (at least three feet) from the outside wall or fence of the primary enclosure to prevent physical contact
between animals inside the enclosure and outside the perimeter fence.
To be corrected by July 12, 2026.

citations.desc: Environment enhancement to promote psychological well-being.
citations.narrative:
The Environment Enhancement Plan does not adequately address the social needs of an individually housed, male
bonnet macaque. While the facility did have a plan for a different individually housed primate, the facility representative
stated that they could not implement that plan with the bonnet macaque. Failure to meet the social needs of primates is
known to cause poor psychological welfare. The environment enhancement plan must include specific provisions to
address the social needs of nonhuman primates of species known to exist in social groups in nature. Such specific
provisions must be in accordance with currently accepted professional standards, as cited in appropriate professional
journals or reference guides, and as directed by the attending veterinarian.
To be corrected by June 26, 2026

There are two enclosures that are not being kept in good repair. In an enclosure housing two raccoons, one of the
enclosure fence support corners is rusted through near the base and one of the lower horizontal enclosure fence bars
have rusted through creating holes with jagged edges that the animals can access. In an enclosure housing the mountain
coati, one of the lower horizontal enclosure fence bars is fully rusted through and has other holes due to rust, there is an
enclosure fence corner from a vertical bar to the lower enclosure fence bar it rusted through, and the den box has a
significant amount of flaking rust on the bottom.
Enclosures that are not kept in good repair, including areas of excessive rust, can result in injury to the animals from
sharp or jagged edges. The facility must be constructed of such material and of such strength as appropriate for the
animals involved. The housing facilities shall be maintained in good repair to protect the animals from injury and to contain
the animals.
To be corrected by July 12, 2026.

Eleven degus in an outdoor enclosure died due to cold weather that occurred overnight between January 15-16, 2026.
The facility owner stated that on the morning of January 16th, an employee discovered that the supplemental heat source
that the facility provided had become disconnected and did not provide warmth to the degus which resulted in death. The
facility has since implemented a new heat source monitoring protocol and alarm system. Inadequate protection from local
climatic conditions could subject the species to unfavorable weather, affecting the health of the animals and creating
unnecessary discomfort or could lead to death. Natural or artificial shelter appropriate to the local climatic conditions for
the species concerned shall be provided for all animals kept outdoors to afford them protection and to prevent discomfort
to such animals.
Corrected at the time of inspection June 11, 2026
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with a facility representative.
